unit: Ch 3: Employee Cost and Direct Expenses
note: AI-written summary of ICAI study material. Check the original for exact wording.

topics.title: Introduction & Classification of Employee Cost
explain: Employee cost or labour cost is the compensation paid to workers for their exertion in manufacturing products or offering services.
It includes basic wages, salaries, allowances, incentives, overtime pay, employer contribution to PF/ESI, and fringe benefits.
Direct employee cost can be directly attributed and allocated to a specific cost object in an economically feasible manner.
Indirect employee cost cannot be directly traced to a specific cost object and is treated as overhead.
Direct employee cost varies with production volume, whereas indirect employee cost may not.

flow.title: Classification of Employee Cost
steps: Incur employee compensation expense
Check direct traceability to cost object
Traceable: Classify as Direct Employee Cost
Non-traceable: Classify as Indirect Employee Cost
Direct goes to Prime Cost, Indirect to Overheads

topics.example: Wages paid to a tailor stitching a shirt are direct employee cost, whereas salary paid to the factory floor supervisor is indirect employee cost.
remember: Direct employee cost varies directly with production volume.
Employer contribution to PF and ESI is part of total employee cost.
mistakes: Excluding employer contributions to PF and welfare funds from total employee cost calculations.

quiz.q: Which of the following is classified as a direct employee cost?
o: Wages of worker operating a production machine
quiz.why: Wages of machine operators are directly traceable to specific product cost objects.

quiz.q: How are indirect employee costs accounted for in cost accounting?
o: Charged to Costing Profit & Loss Account
quiz.why: Indirect employee costs cannot be traced to specific jobs and are treated as overheads.

topics.title: Employee Cost Control & Departmental Functions
explain: Employee cost control aims to keep the wage cost per unit of output as low as possible by encouraging efficiency.
It requires active coordination among five major departments.
Personnel (HR) Department handles recruitment, qualification checks, records maintenance, and training.
Engineering & Work Study Department prepares job specs, supervises work, conducts time & motion studies, and evaluates jobs.
Time-keeping Department maintains attendance records and records time spent on various jobs.
Payroll Department prepares payroll sheets, calculates pay slips, and disburses salary payments.
Cost Accounting Department accumulates, classifies, and allocates labour costs to cost centres.

flow.title: Departmental Sequence for Labour Cost Control
steps: Personnel Dept recruits and trains workers
Engineering Dept sets standard job timings
Time-keeping Dept logs attendance and job hours
Payroll Dept computes wages and deductions
Cost Accounting Dept allocates cost to cost objects

topics.example: The Work Study department determines that assembling a table takes 2 standard hours, while HR ensures qualified carpenters are recruited.
remember: The aim of labour cost control is minimizing wage cost per unit, not minimizing individual worker wages.
Engineering department is responsible for time and motion studies.
mistakes: Confusing the functions of Time-keeping (attendance/job time) with Payroll (wage calculation/disbursement).

quiz.q: Which department is responsible for conducting time and motion studies?
quiz.why: Engineering and Work Study department sets performance standards via time and motion studies.

quiz.q: What is the primary objective of employee cost control?
o: To keep wage cost per unit of output as low as possible
quiz.why: Employee cost control aims at achieving optimum efficiency to keep unit labor cost low.

topics.title: Attendance Procedure (Time-Keeping) & Time-Booking
explain: Time-keeping refers to recording the arrival and departure times of employees to track total attendance.
Time-booking refers to recording the exact time spent by an employee on each specific job or process.
Manual time-keeping methods include Attendance Register method and Metal Disc/Token method.
Mechanical/Automated methods include Punch Card Attendance system and Bio-Metric Attendance system.
Time-booking helps in job costing, measuring worker efficiency, and fixing variance responsibilities.
Job cards can be maintained per job or per worker to reconcile job time with attendance time.

flow.title: Time Recording & Reconciliation Flow
steps: Worker arrives at factory premises
Time-keeping records overall attendance time
Worker begins work on specific assigned jobs
Time-booking records time spent per job
Reconcile job time plus idle time with attendance time

topics.example: Swiping an ID card at the factory gate is time-keeping, whereas logging 4 hours on 'Job X' on a daily job card is time-booking.
remember: Time-keeping measures total factory attendance time.
Time-booking measures specific job or activity time.
mistakes: Assuming time-keeping alone is sufficient for calculating job costs without time-booking records.

quiz.q: What is recorded under time-booking?
o: Total attendance time spent in factory
Time spent by an employee on specific jobs or activities
quiz.why: Time-booking breaks down attendance time into specific jobs and activities.

quiz.q: Which attendance method uses unique physical traits such as fingerprints or facial recognition?
quiz.why: Biometric systems verify unique physical and behavioral traits of employees.

topics.title: Payroll Procedure & Statutory Deductions
explain: Payroll procedure involves computing gross earnings, applying deductions, preparing pay slips, and disbursing net wages.
Time-keeping sends attendance data and HR provides employee rates to the Payroll department.
Statutory deductions include Provident Fund (PF), Employee State Insurance (ESI), TDS, and Professional Tax.
Voluntary deductions include voluntary PF, benevolent fund contributions, loan recoveries, and advance dues.
Cost/Accounting department disburses net salary to employees and deposits statutory dues to government bodies.

flow.title: Payroll Processing Workflow
steps: Collect attendance sheet from Time-keeping
Receive approved wage rates from HR
Compute gross wages including incentives
Subtract statutory and voluntary deductions
Pay net wages and deposit statutory liabilities

topics.example: A worker earns a Gross Pay of ₹16,500. After deducting ₹800 PF and ₹200 ESI, the worker receives a Net Pay of ₹15,500.
remember: Statutory deductions include PF, ESI, TDS, and Professional Tax.
Employers deposit both employee deductions and employer contributions to statutory bodies.
mistakes: Confusing employee's statutory deduction (subtracted from gross wages) with employer's contribution (added to employer cost).

quiz.q: Which of the following is a statutory deduction from gross wages?
quiz.why: Employee contribution to Provident Fund is a mandatory statutory deduction.

quiz.q: Who prepares the wage sheet and payslips for employees?
quiz.why: Payroll department computes wages, prepares payslips, and handles disbursement.

topics.title: Idle Time & Its Accounting Treatment
explain: Idle time is the period for which the worker is paid but no production is carried out (Time Paid minus Time Booked).
Normal idle time is unavoidable in regular operations (e.g., gate-to-workplace walk, setup time, job changes, rest breaks).
Normal idle time cost is treated as production cost by inflating the wage rate for direct workers, or as overheads for indirect workers.
Abnormal idle time arises from abnormal factors (e.g., power failure, breakdown, raw material shortage, strikes, floods).
Abnormal idle time cost is excluded from production cost and charged directly to Costing Profit and Loss Account.

flow.title: Idle Time Treatment Flow
steps: Calculate Idle Time = Time Paid minus Time Booked
Identify root cause of idle time
If normal: Inflate direct hourly rate or include in overheads
If abnormal: Isolate cost of lost hours
Charge abnormal idle cost to Costing P&L Account

topics.example: 30 minutes spent daily on lunch and tea breaks is normal idle time (inflates hourly wage rate). 4 hours lost due to factory power outage is abnormal idle time (charged to Costing P&L).
remember: Normal idle time is absorbed into product cost.
Abnormal idle time is charged to Costing Profit & Loss Account.
mistakes: Charging machine breakdown idle time to product cost instead of Costing Profit & Loss Account.

quiz.q: How is normal idle time of direct workers treated in cost accounting?
o: Charged to Costing Profit and Loss Account
By inflating the hourly wage rate charged to production
quiz.why: Normal idle time is unavoidable and absorbed in production cost via inflated wage rates.

quiz.q: Cost of abnormal idle time caused by raw material shortage is charged to:
quiz.why: Abnormal idle time costs are excluded from product costs and written off to Costing P&L.

topics.title: Overtime Work & Overtime Premium Treatment
explain: Overtime refers to work done beyond normal working hours. Overtime Payment = Normal Wages + Overtime Premium.
Under Section 59 of Factories Act 1948, working >9 hours a day or >48 hours a week entitles workers to double ordinary wage rates.
Ordinary rate includes basic wages plus DA and concessional food sales, but excludes bonus and overtime wages.
If overtime is at customer request: Charge overtime premium directly to that specific job.
If overtime is for general production or urgent orders: Treat overtime premium as departmental overhead cost.
If overtime is due to fault of management/another department: Charge premium to the defaulting department.
If overtime is due to abnormal events (floods, earthquakes): Charge overtime premium to Costing P&L Account.

flow.title: Overtime Premium Treatment Decision
steps: Worker operates beyond 9 hrs/day or 48 hrs/week
Calculate overtime pay at 2x ordinary rate
Identify cause of overtime work
Customer request -> Charge to specific job
General/Abnormal cause -> Charge to Overheads or Costing P&L

topics.example: A worker works 10 hours on Monday. 1 hour is overtime. Basic hourly rate is ₹100. Overtime pay = (1 hr x ₹100 normal) + (1 hr x ₹100 premium) = ₹200.
remember: Factories Act 1948 overtime trigger: >9 hours/day or >48 hours/week.
Overtime premium rate is double the ordinary rate of wages.
mistakes: Including bonus or overtime wages when computing the 'ordinary rate of wages' under Factories Act 1948.

quiz.q: Under the Factories Act 1948, overtime pay at double the ordinary rate is required if a worker works more than:
quiz.why: Section 59 of Factories Act 1948 prescribes overtime pay for work beyond 9 hrs/day or 48 hrs/week.

quiz.q: How is overtime premium treated when overtime is worked at the specific request of a customer?
o: Charged directly to that specific job
Written off to Costing P&L Account
quiz.why: Overtime requested by a customer is directly attributable to that customer's job.

topics.title: Systems of Wage Payment & Incentive Schemes
explain: Time Rate System pays wages based on time worked: Wages = Time Worked × Rate per unit of time.
Straight Piece Rate System pays based on units produced: Wages = Number of units produced × Rate per unit.
Halsey Premium Plan guarantees time wages and pays 50% bonus on time saved: Wages = (Time Taken × Rate) + [50% × (Standard Time - Time Taken) × Rate].
Rowan Premium Plan pays bonus proportional to time saved over standard time: Wages = (Time Taken × Rate) + [(Time Saved / Standard Time) × Time Taken × Rate].
Halsey and Rowan plans give equal bonus when actual time taken is exactly 50% of standard time allowed.
Rowan system protects against loose rate setting as bonus drops when time saved exceeds 50% of standard time.

flow.title: Calculation of Incentive Wages
steps: Determine Standard Time (SH) and Time Taken (AH)
Calculate Time Saved = SH minus AH
If AH >= SH: Pay guaranteed time rate (AH x R)
If Halsey Plan: Add bonus = 50% x Time Saved x R
If Rowan Plan: Add bonus = (Time Saved / SH) x AH x R

topics.example: Standard time = 8 hrs, Time taken = 6 hrs, Rate = ₹60/hr. Halsey earnings = (6x60) + 50%(2x60) = ₹420. Rowan earnings = (6x60) + (2/8 x 6x60) = ₹450.
remember: Halsey Bonus = 50% × Time Saved × Time Rate.
Rowan Bonus = (Time Saved / Standard Time) × Time Taken × Time Rate.
Halsey and Rowan bonus amounts are equal when Time Taken = 50% of Standard Time.
mistakes: Using Actual Time instead of Standard Time in the denominator of the Rowan bonus fraction.

quiz.q: Under Halsey Premium Plan, bonus is calculated as:
o: (Time Saved / Standard Time) × Time Taken × Rate
quiz.why: Halsey Plan pays a 50% bonus on wages of time saved.

quiz.q: The bonus calculated under Halsey Plan and Rowan Plan is equal when actual time taken is:
quiz.why: Both plans yield identical bonus amounts when actual time equals 50% of allowed standard time.

topics.title: Absorption of Wages & Costing Hourly Rate
explain: Total employee wage cost includes basic wages, DA, overtime, bonuses, employer PF/ESI contributions, and non-monetary fringe benefits.
Basic wage is payment for work done measured in hours or units produced.
Dearness Allowance (DA) covers increases in cost of living.
Costing Wage Rate per Hour = Total Estimated Monetary & Non-monetary Benefits / (Budgeted Direct Employee Hours - Normal Idle Time).
Holiday and leave wages are either treated as departmental overheads or absorbed by inflating direct worker wage rates.
Night shift allowance for general factory operations is treated as factory overhead.

flow.title: Costing Hourly Rate Computation
steps: Sum Basic Wages and Dearness Allowance
Add Employer PF, ESI contributions and Bonus
Add non-monetary fringe benefit costs
Calculate Net Effective Hours = Budgeted Hours minus Idle Time
Divide Total Labour Cost by Net Effective Hours

topics.example: Total annual employee cost = ₹1,89,240. Total working days = 300 days of 8 hours, with 15 days paid leave. Effective hours = 285 x 8 = 2,280 hours. Costing rate = ₹1,89,240 / 2,280 = ₹83/hour.
remember: Costing wage rate is computed using net effective working hours.
Night shift allowance for general work is treated as overhead.
mistakes: Dividing total annual labour cost by total calendar hours instead of net effective working hours.

quiz.q: How is night shift allowance treated when incurred for general factory requirements?
o: Charged to Costing Profit & Loss Account
quiz.why: Night shift allowance for general operations cannot be traced to one job and is treated as overhead.

quiz.q: To calculate hourly wage rate for costing purposes, total employee cost is divided by:
o: Total calendar hours in a year
Budgeted direct employee hours minus normal idle time
Gross attendance hours including all leaves
quiz.why: Costing rate per hour uses net effective working hours after deducting normal idle time.

topics.title: Efficiency Rating Procedures & Employee Productivity
explain: Efficiency Rating (%) = (Time Allowed as per Standard / Time Taken) × 100.
If Time Taken <= Standard Time, the worker is rated efficient (Efficiency >= 100%).
If Time Taken > Standard Time, the worker is rated inefficient (Efficiency < 100%).
Employee Productivity Ratio = Standard time for doing actual work / Actual time taken.
Standard time is determined using Time & Motion study or Work study techniques.
Productivity is improved by placing the right person in the right job, training, and work simplification.

flow.title: Efficiency Rating Procedure
steps: Determine standard time using Work Study
Record actual time taken by worker for output
Calculate Efficiency % = (Std Time / Actual Time) x 100
Rate worker as Efficient (>=100%) or Inefficient (<100%)
Use rating for incentive payouts and manpower planning

topics.example: Standard time for a job is 10 hours. Worker completes it in 8 hours. Efficiency rating = (10 / 8) x 100 = 125% (Efficient).
remember: Efficiency % = (Standard Time / Actual Time) × 100.
Productivity measures the input/output ratio of performance.
mistakes: Inverting the efficiency formula as (Actual Time / Standard Time) × 100.

quiz.q: What is the efficiency rating of a worker who completes a job in 6 hours against a standard allowed time of 8 hours?
quiz.why: Efficiency % = (Standard Time / Actual Time) × 100 = (8 / 6) × 100 = 133.33%.

quiz.q: Employee productivity is evaluated by calculating the ratio of:
o: Actual time taken to standard time allowed
Standard time for actual work to actual time taken
Total output units to total wage bill
Normal working hours to overtime hours
quiz.why: Employee productivity ratio is Standard Time for Actual Work divided by Actual Time Taken.

topics.title: Employee (Labour) Turnover & Associated Costs
explain: Employee turnover is the rate of change in the composition of the employee force during a specified period.
Replacement Method = (Number of employees replaced / Average number of employees) × 100. (Excludes new recruits for expansion).
Separation Method = (Number of employees separated / Average number of employees) × 100.
Flux Method = [(Number of separations + Number of replacements) / Average number of employees] × 100, OR [(Separations + Accessions) / Average employees] × 100.
Causes of turnover: Personal (ill health, family), Unavoidable (seasonal, plant relocation), and Avoidable (low wages, bad environment).
Preventive Costs are costs incurred to retain employees (welfare, medical benefits, pensions).
Replacement Costs are costs incurred due to employee departures (recruitment, selection, training, scrap, learning curve loss).

flow.title: Employee Turnover Calculation Flow
steps: Determine average number of workers on roll
Count separations, replacements, and accessions
Calculate rate using Replacement, Separation, or Flux method
Classify causes into Personal, Unavoidable, and Avoidable
Analyze Preventive vs Replacement costs

topics.example: Average workers = 600, Separations = 18, Replacements = 30. Separation Rate = (18/600)x100 = 3%. Replacement Rate = (30/600)x100 = 5%. Flux Rate = [(18+30)/600]x100 = 8%.
remember: Replacement method excludes new employees appointed for expansion plans.
Flux method considers both separations and replacements/accessions.
Turnover costs are divided into Preventive Costs and Replacement Costs.
mistakes: Including new recruitment for expansion as replacements in the Replacement Method formula.

quiz.q: Which method of measuring employee turnover considers both separations and replacements/accessions?
quiz.why: Flux method accounts for both exits (separations) and entries (replacements/accessions).

quiz.q: In calculating labor turnover by the Replacement Method, new workers hired for company expansion are:
quiz.why: Expansion recruits are new additions, not replacements for departed workers.

topics.title: Direct Expenses
explain: Direct expenses are expenses other than direct materials and direct employee costs that are directly traceable to a cost object in an economically feasible manner.
Examples include royalty paid for production, equipment hire charges for a specific job, and product-specific design/blueprint costs.
Direct expenses are measured at invoice/agreed price net of trade discounts/rebates, plus non-creditable duties/taxes and incidental expenses.
Sub-contracting job charges plus value of materials supplied by principal are measured as direct expenses.
Direct expenses form part of Prime Cost. Insignificant direct expenses may be treated as overheads.
Lump-sum payments are amortized over the estimated production volume or benefit period.

flow.title: Direct Expense Identification & Allocation
steps: Incur expense other than material and labour
Check direct traceability to specific job/product
If directly traceable and material: Classify as Direct Expense
If lump-sum: Amortize over production volume
Add Direct Expenses to Prime Cost

topics.example: Paying ₹1,40,000 for a product blueprint specifically drawn for Job A is a direct expense added to Job A's prime cost.
remember: Prime Cost = Direct Material Cost + Direct Employee Cost + Direct Expenses.
Equipment hire charges for a specific job are direct expenses.
mistakes: Classifying general office administration costs or general marketing manager salaries as direct expenses.

quiz.q: Where are direct expenses included in a traditional cost sheet?
quiz.why: Prime Cost equals Direct Materials + Direct Employee Cost + Direct Expenses.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an example of a direct expense?
o: Equipment hire charges paid for a specific job
quiz.why: Equipment hire for a specific job is directly traceable to that job as a direct expense.
